Fiscal restraint or political wedge? Angus Taylor's $31B slash sparks party friction.
Evidence: Budget cuts, backbench pushback, climate funding friction.
#AusPol #Economy #Aletheia

The Coalition plan to cut $31 billion by slashing climate/housing programs and public service jobs aims to restore fiscal responsibility.

The policy triggers backbench dissent and exposes deep rifts over gutting climate agencies and public service jobs while maintaining emissions targets.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.6, -0.5) — Lesser Evil

A fiscal strategy masking partisan wedge politics creates internal fractures and undermines climate commitments.

Liberal ACT Senate candidate Nick Tyrrell has struggled to defend Opposition Leader Angus Taylor's policy to save $31 billion by slashing Labor climate and housing programs and cutting federal public service jobs, as cracks emerge in his party room.

Login or signup to continue reading

When asked if he shared Liberal senator Andrew McLachlan's view that the Coalition plan to cut the resourcing of climate agencies was "illogical" - and if this was in line with his moderate beliefs - Mr Tyrrell sat on the fence.

"Every dollar of climate spending should actually cut emissions, and every dollar of taxpayer money should be carefully spent," he told The Canberra Times, while not specifically backing the plan.

Senator McLachlan told ABC radio on Tuesday that he was "totally opposed" and that with the Coalition still committed to Australia's Paris agreement emission reduction target, it would not make sense to tamper with climate agencies.

While it might deliver a financial saving, he asked, "at what cost to the environment?"

The backbencher said that while he "could be criticised for being too outspoken," there were "many like-minded individuals" in the Liberal party room.

"The community wants to hear from someone on the Liberal side who is committed to reconciling with nature," he said.

Mr Tyrrell, a progressive Liberal who last month stood next to Mr Taylor at his Canberra press conference to announce the $31 billion savings plan, told this masthead: "Andrew's right that it's a false choice: you can take emissions seriously AND still expect value for money."

He said Australians "want to see the receipts" for Labor's climate spending and that the government had failed to deliver, pointing out that Senator Gallagher and Treasurer Jim Chalmers were foreshadowing public sector cuts in next month's mid-year budget update.

Dr Chalmers said on Tuesday that the "substantial savings package" being finalised would respond to "the inflationary pressures in our economy right now," as the government comes under criticism that its spending is fuelling the problem of demand outstripping productivity.
